an expert in increasing the efficient use of machines and personnel

efficient.e: 1398, “making,” from Old French, from Latin efficientem, nominative efficiēns, participle of efficere (“work out, accomplish”) (see effect). Meaning “productive, skilled” is from 1787. Efficiency apartment is first recorded 1930, American English.

s.d: (obsolete) A cause; something that causes an effect.
x: Some are without efficient, as God; others without matter, as Angels […].

s.d: being effective without wasting time or effort or expense
x: an efficient production manager
efficient engines save gas

s.d: able to accomplish a purpose; functioning effectively
x: people who will do nothing unless they get something out of it for themselves are often highly effective persons …
effective personnel

s.d: Making good, thorough, or careful use of resources; not consuming extra. Especially, making good use of time or energy.
x: An efficient process would automate all the routine work.
Our cleaners are almost too efficient: they throw away anything left out on a desk.

s.d: Expressing the proportion of consumed energy that was successfully used in a process; the ratio of useful output to total input.
x: The motor is only 20% efficient at that temperature.

s.d: Causing effects, producing results; bringing into being; initiating change (rare except in philosophical and legal expression efficient cause = causative factor or agent).
x: Ownership, maintenance, or use of the automobile need not be the direct and efficient cause of the injury sustained
It was well said of Plotinus, that the stars were significant, but not efficient.

s.d: effective, efficacious
x: The Efficient Cause is that from which emanates the force that produces the Effect

efficiently.e:
Etymology tree
English efficient
Middle English -ly
English -ly
English efficiently
From efficient + -ly.

s.d: with efficiency; in an efficient manner
x: he functions efficiently

effigy.e: From French effigie, from Latin effigiēs (“likeness, effigy”), from effingō (“represent, portray”).

s.d: a representation of a person (especially in the form of sculpture)
x: the coin bears an effigy of Lincoln
the emperor's tomb had his image carved in stone

s.d: A dummy or other crude representation of a person, group or object that is hated.
x: In England on Bonfire Night, an effigy is often burned.

s.d: A likeness of a person.
x: tomb effigy
All around, terrace by terrace, there went marble lawns well guarded by onyx lions and carved with effigies of all the gods striding amid the symbols of the worlds.

effleurage.e: Borrowed from French effleurage, from effleurer (“to stroke lightly”).

s.d: a rhythmic stroking
x: effleurage of the abdomen is used in the Lamaze method of childbirth

s.d: (uncountable) A form of massage involving smooth strokes of the skin with one's hands.
x: When shampoo is spread on to the hair it is called an effleurage massage movement.

s.d: To gently stroke the skin in a circular motion with the palm of one's hands.

effloresce.e: From Latin efflōrēscere, present active infinitive of efflōrēscō (“to bloom, blossom; to flourish”) + -ere (suffix forming infinitives). Efflōrēscō is derived from ef- (variant of ex- (prefix meaning ‘away; out’)) + flōrēscō (“to blossom, flower; to begin to flourish or prosper”) (from flōreō (“to bloom, blossom, flower; to flourish, prosper”) (from flōs (“blossom, flower”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰleh₃- (“bloom, flower”)) + -scō (suffix forming verbs having the sense of beginning

s.d: come into or as if into flower
x: These manifestations effloresced in the past

s.d: assume crystalline form; become crystallized
become encrusted with crystals due to evaporation
To burst into bloom; to flower.
(figuratively) Of something hidden: to come forth, to emerge; also, to reach full glory or power.
x: These [God's promises], implanted in the soul of David, effloresced in the Psalms to that luxuriance and fruitfulness which have made them the delight and nourishment of all succeeding ages of the church, [...]
No more in tears / She lingers 'mong the years, / No more she watcheth through the lonesome night; / Her night is past, / No shadow on her cast, / She effloresceth 'mong the flowers in light.

s.d: Senses relating to chemistry.: Of a substance: to change from being crystalline to powdery by losing water of crystallization.
x: This is the very caſe with the Pyrites that conſiſt only of iron and ſulphur; yet ſome of them, as we ſaid before, do not effloreſce ſpontaneouſly and turn to Vitriol.
The baryta-salt dried up to a gummy mass, but after a while swelled up in cauliflower-like tufts, which effloresced and fell to pieces on exposure to the air.

s.d: Senses relating to chemistry.: Of a salt: to seep through some material (bricks, concrete, earth, rock, etc.) in a dissolved state, and then crystallize on a surface in a powdery form.
x: The ſalts which effloreſce from old walls, are nitre more or leſs pure, quadrangular nitre, mineral alkali in abundance, more or leſs pure, and mixed with calcareous earth; [...]
It [sodium sulphate] exists likewise native in mineral springs, and sometimes it effloresces on the walls of old buildings.

s.d: Senses relating to chemistry.: Of the surface of a material: to become covered with a powdery salt (as described in sense 3.2).
x: This ſtone is perpetually effloreſcing, and forming the ſalt called Sulphate of Iron: vulgarly, Copperas.
[W]e have seen aluminum parts exposed to magnesium chloride (a common road salt in the northern states and Canada) effloresce so badly they resembled a blossoming, metallic flower!

efflorescence.e: Borrowed from French efflorescence, from Latin efflōrēscō (from ex- (“out”) + flōrēscō (“to blossom”)) + -ence. By surface analysis, effloresce + -ence.

s.d: the period of greatest prosperity or productivity
any red eruption of the skin
the time and process of budding and unfolding of blossoms
a powdery deposit on a surface
(uncountable) The production of flowers.
(figuratively, uncountable) Rapid flowering of a culture or civilisation etc.
(uncountable) The formation of a powdery surface on crystals, as a hydrate is converted to anhydrous form by losing loosely bound water of crystallization to the atmosphere.

(uncountable) An encrustation of soluble salts, commonly white, deposited on the surface of stone, brick, plaster, or mortar; usually caused by free alkalies leached from mortar or adjacent concrete as moisture moves through it.
(uncountable) An encrustation of soluble salts, deposited on rock or soil by evaporation; often found in arid or geothermal environments.
x: I’d hoped that when the black hole of the Donald Trump presidency ended, redirected energy might allow for a cultural efflorescence. So far that hasn’t happened.

s.d: (uncountable) A redness, rash, or eruption on the skin.

efflorescent.e: From Latin efflōrēscēns. Compare French efflorescent. By surface analysis, effloresce + -ent.

s.d: when the bud, or buds, on a plant are bursting into flower
x: The hawthorn tree was abloom in late spring.

s.d: Bursting into flower.
Growing at a rapid rate; flourishing.
Forming a white dust or efflorescence on the surface.

effluence.e: From French effluence, from Latin effluentia.

s.d: the process of flowing out
(uncountable) Something that flows out; the issue.
x: But we have grounds to believe, that there are yet other Rays or Effluences from the Sun, which neither Feeling nor Sight can apprehend, but which are to be inferred from the effects.

effluent.e: From French effluent, from Latin effluens, effluentis. By surface analysis, e- + fluent.

s.d: water mixed with waste matter
A stream that flows out, such as from a lake or reservoir; an outflow; effluence.
x: The landscape was dotted with reservoirs and many many effluent streams.

s.d: (uncountable) Sewage or waste water discharged into a natural body of water.
x: Residents have little control over the industrial effluent that pollutes their rivers.

One of the hidden glories of Victorian engineering is proper drains. Isolating a city’s effluent and shipping it away in underground sewers has probably saved more lives than any medical procedure except vaccination.

s.d: that is flowing outward
Flowing out; outflowing.

effluvium.e: From Latin effluvium (“an outlet”), from effluō (“flow out or away”), from ex (“out of, from”) + fluō (“flow”).

s.d: a foul-smelling outflow or vapor (especially a gaseous waste)
(uncountable) A gaseous or vaporous emission, especially a foul-smelling one.
x: It was the mere effluvium of the flame, the subtle ether that it cast off as it passed, working on us, and making us feel strong as giants and swift as eagles.

And he breathed the breath of the house—a dank savour rather than a smell—a cold, musty effluvium as from underground vaults mingled with the reeking exhalations of linoleum and mildewed and rotten woodwork.

s.d: (uncountable) A condition causing the shedding of hair.
x: Reversible hair loss or effluvium occurs following either endogenous or exogenous damage to anagen hair follicles[…].

efflux.e: From Latin effluxus, from effluō (“flow out or away”), from ex (“out of, from”) + fluō (“flow”). See also effluxion.

s.d: the process of flowing out
(uncountable) Something which has flowed out.
x: the efflux of a boil
Prime cheerer, light! […] Efflux divine.

s.d: To run out; to flow forth.
(obsolete) To pass away.

effort.e:
From Middle French effort, from Old French esfort, deverbal of esforcier (“to force, exert”), from Vulgar Latin *exfortiō, from Latin ex + fortis (“strong”).
Compare typologically Bulgarian усилие (usilie), Czech úsilí, Polish wysiłek, Russian уси́лие (usílije) (< Proto-Slavic *sila).

s.d: earnest and conscientious activity intended to do or accomplish something
x: made an effort to cover all the reading material
wished him luck in his endeavor

s.d: use of physical or mental energy; hard work
x: he got an A for effort
they managed only with great exertion

s.d: a notable achievement
x: he performed a great feat
the book was her finest effort

s.d: a series of actions advancing a principle or tending toward a particular end
x: he supported populist campaigns
they worked in the cause of world peace

s.d: The work involved in performing an activity; exertion.
x: make an effort
take a lot of effort

s.d: An endeavor.
x: Although he didn't win any medals, Johnson's effort at the Olympics won over many fans.

s.d: A force acting on a body in the direction of its motion.
x: the two bodies between which the effort acts

s.d: To make an effort.
(obsolete) To strengthen, fortify or stimulate
x: When old, he lived in London where, being High-minded and Poor, he was exposed to the contempt of disingenuous persons. Yet he efforted his Spirits with a Commemoration of the Days of Old.

s.d: requiring great physical effort
Requiring or showing effort.
x: It is obvious, therefore, that syntopical reading is the most active and effortful kind of reading.

s.d: requiring or apparently requiring no effort
x: the swallows glided in an effortless way through the busy air

s.d: not showing effort or strain
x: a difficult feat performed with casual mastery
casual grace

s.d: Without effort.
x: She made the move look completely effortless.

Middle English -ly
English -ly
English effortlessly
From effortless + -ly.

s.d: without effort or apparent effort
x: she danced gracefully and effortlessly
swallows gliding effortlessly through the air

s.d: Without effort; without difficulty or struggle.
x: She hoisted the child effortlessly and plopped him in bed.

s.d: the quality of requiring little effort
x: such effortlessness is achieved only after hours of practice

s.d: (uncountable) The state of being effortless; facility.

effrontery.e: From late 17th century French effronterie, from effronté (“shameless, insolent”), from Old French esfronté, from Vulgar Latin *exfrontātus. Compare Latin effrōns (“barefaced”), from the prefix ex- (“from”) + frōns (“forehead”) (English: front). By surface analysis, ef- + front + -er + -y.

s.d: audacious (even arrogant) behavior that you have no right to
x: he despised them for their presumptuousness

s.d: (uncountable) Insolent and shameless audacity.
x: We even had the effrontery to suggest that he should leave the country.

Let not the Englishman in Scotland believe that the undoffed hat, the curt reply, the apparent assumption of equality, all spring from deliberate effrontery, and are wholly beyond the reach of southern influence.

effulgence.e: From Latin ex- (“out of, from”) and fulgere (“to shine”). By surface analysis, ef- + Latin fulg(ere) + -ence.

s.d: the quality of being bright and sending out rays of light
(uncountable) A state of being bright and radiant, splendor, brilliance.
x: […] the clear effulgence of the stars by night […]
He stood for a moment taking in the effulgence.

effulgent.e: From Latin effulgēns (“flashing, glittering”), present participle of effulgeō (“to shine or gleam forth, flash, glitter”), from ē- (variant of ex- (prefix meaning ‘out; away’)) + fulgeō (“to flash, gleam, glisten, glitter, shine”) (from Proto-Indo-European *bʰel- (“shiny; white”)). By surface analysis, ef- + Latin fulg(ere) + -ent.

s.d: radiating or as if radiating light
x: the beaming sun
the effulgent daffodils

s.d: (figuratively, literary) Radiant, resplendent, shining.
x: Margaret, aged six, entered her kindergarten after many days' absence, with so effulgent a face as must kindle curiosity in the dullest.
Except for the faintest tinge of olive, her cheeks were colorless, yet they spoke of perfect health, and shone with that same pale, effulgent glow, like the reflection of a late sun.

effuse.e: Borrowed from Middle French effuser, from Latin effusus, past participle of effundere (“to pour out”).

s.d: (obsolete) effusion; loss
x: Much effuse of blood.

s.d: pour out liberally
x: effused brine

s.d: flow or spill forth
give out or emit (also metaphorically)
x: The room effuses happiness

s.d: To emit; to give off.
(figuratively) To gush; to be excitedly talkative and enthusiastic about something.
To pour out like a stream or freely; to cause to exude; to shed.
x: With gushing blood effused.

s.d: To leak out through a small hole.
Poured out freely; profuse.
x: So should our joy be very effuse.

s.d: Disposed to pour out freely; prodigal.
x: No wanton waste amid effuse expence

s.d: Spreading loosely, especially on one side.
x: an effuse inflorescence

s.d: Having the lips, or edges, of the aperture abruptly spreading, as in certain shells.

effusion.e: Borrowed from Middle French effusion, from Latin effūsiō (“outpouring”). Displaced native Old English āgotennes.

s.d: an unrestrained expression of emotion
flow under pressure
(uncountable) A liquid outpouring.
(uncountable) Process of gases passing through a hole or holes considerably smaller than the mean free path of the gas molecules.
(figuratively, uncountable) An outpouring of speech or emotion.
x:
1930; George S. Kaufman, Morrie Ryskind, Bert Kalmar, Harry Ruby; Animal Crackers, Paramount Pictures
Captain Spaulding: My friends, I am highly gratified by this magnificent display of effusion […]
The housekeeper, a very decorative brunette of thirty-five with a pseudo-English accent, greeted him with a mixture of grateful effusion and condescending patronage.

s.d: (uncountable) The seeping of fluid into a body cavity; the fluid itself.
x: pleural effusion

s.d: uttered with unrestrained enthusiasm
x: a novel told in burbly panting tones

s.d: extravagantly demonstrative
x: insincere and effusive demonstrations of sentimental friendship
a large gushing female

s.d: Gushy; unrestrained, extravagant or excessive (in emotional expression).
x: effusive praise

s.d: (archaic) Pouring, spilling out freely; overflowing.
x: wash'd with the effusive wave

s.d: Extrusive; having solidified after being poured out as molten lava.

x: the critics praised her effusively

eft.e: From Middle English evete, from Old English efete, of unknown origin.

s.d: a newt in its terrestrial stage of development
A newt, especially a smooth newt (Lissotriton vulgaris, syn. Triturus punctatus), of Europe.
x: Only these marishes and myrie bogs, / In which the fearefull ewftes do build their bowres, / Yeeld me an hostry mongst the croking frogs […].

How did he like it when the live creatures
Tickled and toused and browsed him all over,
And worm, slug, eft, with serious features
Came in, each one, for his right of trover?

s.d: (obsolete) Again; afterwards
x: And when they were all gone, / And the dim moon doth eft withhold the light,[…]
